Gregorian chant, also called plainsong or plainchant, is the monophonic liturgical singing tradition of the Roman Catholic Church, codified in the sixth through eighth centuries and traditionally attributed to Pope Gregory I, though modern scholarship shows it developed gradually. Sung in unison without instrumental accompaniment, Gregorian chant uses Latin texts, modal melodies, and a free, speech-like rhythm aligned to liturgical needs rather than metrical regularity.

Gregorian chant emerged from earlier Christian liturgical traditions and Jewish cantorial practice. It became the standardized music for the Mass and the Office—daily prayers—throughout the medieval Catholic Church. The tradition was monophonic—a single melodic line sung by all voices in unison—as opposed to the later development of polyphonic, multi-voiced church music. This allowed congregational participation and clarity of the sacred text.

Notation evolved from early neumes, symbolic marks indicating pitch direction without specifying absolute pitch, to the four-line staff, allowing exact transcription and transmission of melodies across centuries. Gregorian chant uses the eight church modes, also called Gregorian modes, each with a different final note and range, somewhat analogous to minor and major keys but with distinct characteristics. These modes carry liturgical significance.

The rhythm of Gregorian chant is free and prose-like, not metrically regular. Singers follow the natural phrasing of Latin text and liturgical function, allowing for rubato and expressive freedom within the fixed melodic skeleton. Some composers working in the plainsong tradition expanded its expressive range through subtle ornamentation and elaborate melismatic passages—multiple notes on a single syllable—while maintaining the unaccompanied, monophonic character.

Gregorian chant had declined by the nineteenth century but was revived in the late eighteen-hundreds as the Church sought to restore liturgical authenticity. Modern Catholic Mass still uses simplified Gregorian melodies, keeping alive this ancient tradition that served as the foundation for all later Western polyphonic music.
